changes.before: Define onlyFirst(_ first: [String], _ second: [String]) -> [String]. Return distinct values present only in first, sorted for display.
changes.after: Compare two sets to find shared values or values found in only one.

before: union returns values present in either set. intersection returns values present in both. Set(morningItems) constructs a Set from the array and removes repeated equal values. Each result is another Set, so duplicates are not repeated and iteration order is not a display promise. sorted() converts the result into a predictable ordered array for these String examples.

morning.subtracting(evening) returns morning’s values that are absent from evening. Reversing the operands can change the result. These nonmutating operations leave morning and evening unchanged; mutating alternatives have different names and are outside this lesson.

```swift
let morningItems = ["draw", "walk", "draw"]
let morning = Set(morningItems)
let evening: Set<String> = ["walk", "read"]
print(morning.union(evening).sorted())
print(morning.intersection(evening).sorted())
print(morning.subtracting(evening).sorted())
print(morning.sorted())
```
Output:
```text
["draw", "read", "walk"]
["walk"]
["draw"]
["draw", "walk"]
```

```swift
let morningItems = ["draw", "walk", "draw"]
let morning = Set(morningItems)
let evening: Set<String> = ["swim"]
print(morning.union(evening).sorted())
print(morning.intersection(evening).sorted())
print(morning.subtracting(evening).sorted())
print(morning.sorted())
```
Output:
```text
["draw", "swim", "walk"]
[]
["draw", "walk"]
["draw", "walk"]
```
Comparing two lists of chosen activities can reveal shared choices or choices unique to one list. Convert arrays to sets only when repeated occurrences should no longer matter.
after: `union` returns values found in either set. `intersection` returns values found in both. Each result is a Set, so matching values appear only once.
`first.subtracting(second)` keeps values in the first set that are absent from the second. The direction matters: swapping the sets can give a different answer.

```swift
let morningItems = ["draw", "walk", "draw"]
let morning = Set(morningItems)
let evening: Set<String> = ["walk", "read"]
print(morning.union(evening).sorted())
print(morning.intersection(evening).sorted())
print(morning.subtracting(evening).sorted())
print(morning.sorted())
```
The union is draw, read, walk. The intersection is walk. Subtracting evening from morning leaves draw. The final print confirms morning still contains draw and walk.

These methods return new sets without changing the original sets. `sorted()` turns each result into an ordered array for display. Convert arrays to sets only when repeated occurrences should count as one value.
